title: The Book of Life
hook: Can Jesus erase your name from the Book of Life and send you to hellfire?
tldr: No. In Scripture the Book of Life lists the living, and in Sardis, citizen rosters dropped names at death or disgrace. Revelation 3:5 is a litotes: an understatement promising special honor to overcomers, not a threat of lost salvation or eternal torture.
big_idea: Revelation 3:5 promises honor to the faithful, not torment to the rest.

points.title: Revelation speaks in symbols
points.text: Revelation is apocalyptic, full of beasts, dragons and flying horses that first-century readers would not take literally. Its vivid images convey spiritual truths rather than literal descriptions.

points.title: A book of the living
points.text: In the Hebrew Scriptures the Book of the Living lists those presently alive on earth, righteous or wicked. Whatever the book, those written in it are alive.

points.title: Sardis kept citizen rosters
points.text: Towns like Sardis listed their citizens. A name was removed at death, or when someone committed severe crimes and shamed the town. Jesus used an image the readers knew.

points.title: White garments mean honor
points.text: Sardis was famous for wool and dyed fabrics. White garments signified honor, festivity and victory. The promise to overcomers is special recognition for faithful service.

points.title: A litotes, not a threat
points.text: Since Jesus taught eternal life cannot be lost, 'I will not blot out his name' is an understatement that affirms honor by negating its opposite. Failing to overcome means forfeiting the Master's 'Well done.'

sections.summary: Revelation is steeped in symbolism and metaphor, written in the apocalyptic genre. It describes beasts, dragons, flying horses and other images first-century readers would not have taken literally. The genre uses vivid imagery and symbolic language to convey deeper spiritual truths, not literal descriptions.

Revelation 3:5 says the overcomer will be clothed in white garments and his name will not be blotted out of the Book of Life, and Jesus will confess his name before the Father and the angels. Many Christians fear it implies Jesus might erase names already written, meaning loss of eternal life and torture in hellfire. The words were addressed to the church in Sardis.

sections.h: What is the Book of Life?
sections.summary: In the Hebrew Scriptures the Book of the Living lists those presently alive on earth, righteous or wicked. It appears three ways: the Book of the Living (Psalm 69:28), the Book of Life (Philippians 4:3; Revelation 3:5; 20:12, 15) and the Lamb's Book of Life (Revelation 13:8; 21:27). Either way, those written are alive. Some see two books, one listing all the living and one listing those receiving great honor; others see one book.

In John's time, many towns including Sardis kept citizenship rosters. When a person died, the name was removed. A person who committed severe crimes and brought great shame on the town might also be removed. Scripture does speak of names being blotted out, but this does not mean losing eternal life.

An overcomer faithfully loves, serves and honors Jesus throughout life. The promise never to remove an overcomer's name is a tribute of great honor and respect, special recognition for faithful service. It does not mean those who fail to overcome are tortured in hellfire or lose eternal life. Sardis boasted of woolen goods and dyed fabrics, and white garments connoted honor, festivity and victory.

Jesus taught eternal life can never be lost (John 3:15-18; 4:10-14; 5:24; 6:35-40; 10:28-29; 11:25-26), so 'I will not blot out his name' is best read as litotes: an understatement affirming something by negating its opposite. Saying 'I will not stop loving my wife as long as she makes me ice cream' stresses love, not a condition. Jesus uses a familiar image to stress honor for the faithful, not fire for others.

Not having one's name acknowledged simply means forfeiting the Master's 'Well done,' the commendation given to faithful servants in Jesus' parables. It is a loss of honor and reward, not a sentence of eternal torment.
